description: We're a team SentinelX  building an interactive map that ranks Earth locations matching Moon base and Mars conditions, using NASA open data. These analog sites let space agencies test habitats, rovers and procedures before real missions. We're looking for teammates in GIS/remote sensing, Python data analysis, web mapping and design or storytelling. All skill levels welcome, no space background needed. Join us!
summary:
Before astronauts go to the Moon or Mars, teams test their equipment and plans in places on Earth that look and feel similar, like the Atacama Desert or the Arctic. But most teams keep going back to the same few famous spots, and there’s no easy way to tell which place on Earth best matches a particular landing site.

We built SentinelX, a website with an interactive globe that does exactly that. You pick a destination, such as Gale Crater on Mars or a lava-tube pit on the Moon, and it ranks 51 places on Earth by how closely they match, using NASA climate data and the ground conditions at each site. It explains every score, compares each site with the real destination, and can scan any part of the globe for new matches.

It also points out promising places almost nobody has studied yet, like a desert lava tube in Saudi Arabia that beat every well-known site for the Moon
details:
What it does
SentinelX is a website that helps answer one question: which places on Earth are the best practice grounds for a specific landing site on the Moon or Mars?

You choose one of five destinations: Jezero Crater, Gale Crater or Arcadia Planitia on Mars, or the South Pole or the Marius Hills lava-tube pit on the Moon. The site then ranks 51 places on Earth by how closely they match it, shown on a spinning 3D globe and in a list. Click any place to see why it scored the way it did, or compare it side by side with the real destination on a radar chart.

How it works
Every place gets a score from 0 to 100 based on two things. The first is its climate: how hot or cold it is, how much the temperature swings between day and night, how much it rains, how dry and thin the air is, and how strong the sunlight is. This comes live from NASA’s POWER climate data. The second is its ground: whether it has volcanic rock, impact craters, lava tubes and caves, salt flats, old lake beds, frozen ground or sand dunes. We rated these from published descriptions of each site.

Each destination cares about different things. Ground ice and cold matter most for Arcadia Planitia, for example, while lava tubes and volcanic rock matter most for the Marius Hills pit. The site weighs each factor to match, and users can move sliders to change those weights. You can also click anywhere on land, or scan a whole region, to fetch NASA climate data for those spots and see how well they match.

What we found
The famous test sites came out near the top where experts would expect. Haughton Crater in the Canadian Arctic ranks highest for the Moon’s South Pole, and the McMurdo Dry Valleys in Antarctica for Mars’s icy plains, which tells us the method makes sense. The surprises are places almost nobody has studied. A desert lava tube in Saudi Arabia called Umm Jirsan scored higher than every well-known site for the Moon’s lava-tube pit. Tso Kar, a cold salt lake high in Ladakh, India, was the best little-known match for all three Mars destinations.

Why it matters
Testing on Earth is much cheaper and safer than finding problems on the Moon or Mars. SentinelX gives mission teams, space agencies and students a free, open way to choose test sites that match their actual target, instead of always going back to the same few famous places. It also shows countries good test sites close to home that they may have overlooked.

Tools we used
We built the website with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, using the D3.js library for the globe and charts. Climate data comes from NASA’s POWER service, the world map from Natural Earth, and facts about each destination from NASA and JAXA missions such as Perseverance, Curiosity, the Mars Reconnaissance Orbiter, the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter and Kaguya. We used an AI assistant (Claude) to help build the website and write the text.

What makes it creative
Most comparisons just call a place “Mars-like”. SentinelX asks “like which part of Mars?” and scores every site against a specific landing target. It also treats “nobody has studied this yet” as a reason to look, so the globe becomes a guide to where to explore next.

What we kept in mind
No place on Earth has Mars’s thin air or the Moon’s lack of atmosphere, so a score compares Earth sites with each other rather than claiming a perfect match. NASA’s climate data covers areas about 50 km across, not a single rock. Our ground ratings are our own judgment from what has been published. Next, we want to replace them with satellite maps of terrain and minerals, so the scan can find good geology as well as good climate.
